findings.paper_title: First Quarter Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27
findings.headline: Commercial waste and recycling income red-flagged: £12k shortfall driven by ongoing structural decline in customer base
findings.detail: Commercial refuse and recycling income is forecast £12k below budget (£1.306m budget, £1.294m forecast). This reflects a steady decline in customer numbers (down 0.1% year-on-year). The council recommended and received approval for a permanent reduction to this income budget, and new UK Simpler Recycling rules have only partially offset the underlying decline through mandatory food waste collections.
findings.matters: A key revenue line is in structural decline despite regulatory changes; income from this source may continue to erode
findings.figures: £1.306m original budget; £1.294m forecast; 902 customers (down from 903 prior year)
findings.quote: The red indicator relating to the forecast shortfall for Commercial waste and recycling income in comparison to the original budget is indicative of the steady decline in the size of the customer base.

findings.paper_title: First Quarter Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27
findings.headline: IT development projects deferred by Local Government Reorganization: £45k of planning software budget carried forward for second year
findings.detail: Idox Insights installation (£20k) and Agile AI procurement (£25k) have been deferred pending LGR decisions. Agile AI was paused after Hertfordshire County Council decided not to lead the procurement and other council collaboration stalled due to LGR. Idox deferred awaiting LGR clarity. Both are being carried forward again, indicating persistent uncertainty.
findings.matters: LGR is causing material disruption to planned technology investments and business improvements; carry-forward for a second year suggests these may not proceed at all
findings.figures: £45k deferred (£20k Idox Insights + £25k Agile AI)
findings.quote: The installation of Idox Insights has also been deferred pending decisions on LGR. It is requested that the allocated budget is carried forward again as these may progress once LGR decisions clarify matters.

findings.paper_title: First Quarter Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27
findings.headline: Efficiency programme running 2% behind target at end of Quarter One: £59k net underachievement against £2.894m plan
findings.detail: The council approved £2.894m in efficiency savings for 2026/27. At end of Q1, £59k of underachievement is forecast: £21k from Solar for Business closure and £25k from Careline service desk no longer generating in-house savings. This represents early slippage that could indicate full-year underperformance.
findings.matters: Efficiency savings are critical to the financial plan; early-year shortfalls suggest the council may miss annual targets and face funding pressure
findings.figures: £2.894m total efficiencies approved; £59k net underachievement
findings.quote: The current forecast at the end of Quarter One is a net underachievement of £59k. This relates to: Income from Solar for Business scheme, as highlighted in table three above. £21k underachievement.

findings.paper_title: First Quarter Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27
findings.headline: Solar for Business Initiative closed without any installations; generated zero income against £21k budgeted
findings.detail: The Solar for Business Initiative has been closed without completing any installations due to inability to attract suitable business interest. The scheme has generated no revenue and represents a £21k income shortfall and elimination of a planned efficiency saving.
findings.matters: A revenue-generating initiative failed to attract market uptake, indicating planned income was optimistic or the market for this product is weak
findings.figures: £21k budgeted income; £0 actual outturn
findings.quote: This project was closed without any installations being completed, due to difficulties in attracting suitable business interest. As a result, the scheme has not generated any income.

findings.paper_title: First Quarter Revenue Budget Monitoring 2026/27
findings.headline: Careline service desk system: planned in-house development cancelled; now requires external procurement at significantly higher ongoing cost
findings.detail: The council budgeted for an in-house development of a service desk management system with an associated £25k annual efficiency saving. Due to complexity and technical resources being consumed by Local Government Reorganization (LGR), the council must now procure the system externally. Beyond losing the £25k efficiency, ongoing support and maintenance costs from the market are now significantly higher than originally estimated because the market has shifted to subscription-based cloud platforms.
findings.matters: A planned efficiency saving has been eliminated and replaced with higher costs, reducing financial capacity and suggesting LGR is materially disrupting normal operations
findings.figures: £25k efficiency lost; additional costs for external procurement and subscription-based support now required
findings.quote: The solution was intended to be developed in-house, with an associated ongoing efficiency of £25k earmarked from 2026/27; however, due to its complexity and the technical resource absorbed with supporting LGR, it must now be procured externally.

findings.paper_title: NHDC BBA - report for FARC
findings.headline: Rebuild work will cost £26,500 for risk assessment plus an estimated £15,000–£25,000 for substantive remedial work.
findings.detail: KPMG's risk assessment fees of £26,500 plus VAT have been agreed with the Director of Resources and are subject to PSAA approval. The substantive phase (actual audit work to resolve the identified issues) is estimated at £15,000–£25,000. Total rebuild costs are therefore likely to exceed £40,000 before VAT.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted or escalating audit fees represent a cost pressure on the council and reduce capacity for service investment.
findings.figures: Risk assessment: £26,500 plus VAT; Substantive phase: £15,000–£25,000
findings.quote: We note our fees for the risk assessment phase of work are £26,500 (plus VAT). These have been agreed with the Director-Resources and are now subject to PSAA approval. The fees for the substantive phase are likely to be in the range of £15,000 to £25,000.

findings.paper_title: NHDC BBA - report for FARC
findings.headline: Risk assessment identified unverified reserves movements and property asset accounting as the key areas requiring rebuild work.
findings.detail: Transfers to and from unusable reserves and earmarked reserves were not appropriately identified or classified during 2022/23 and 2023/24. Similarly, property, plant and equipment revaluation adjustments and capitalisation decisions may not have been correctly recorded. KPMG will verify these balance sheet items against supporting evidence, fixed asset registers, and approved reserve decisions in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Reserves management and asset accounting directly affect the council's stated financial position. Weaknesses in these areas, if material, would affect covenant calculations and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Four balance sheet captions flagged: Unusable Reserves, Earmarked Reserves, Property plant and equipment (revaluation), Property plant and equipment (additions)
findings.quote: The risk assessment has identified risks of material misstatement. We need to complete procedures to address these risks.

findings.paper_title: NHDC BBA - report for FARC
findings.headline: Council had disclaimed audit opinions for three consecutive years (2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25) but has been assessed as straightforward to rebuild.
findings.detail: The council's predecessor auditor disclaimed the 2022/23 opinion, and KPMG issued disclaimers for 2023/24 (February 2025) and 2024/25 (February 2026) due to government backstop arrangements. KPMG has now completed a risk assessment for the 2025/26 audit and categorised the council as Category A—'audits expected to be relatively straightforward and able to sustain an ISA-compliant approach without significant difficulty'—rather than the higher-difficulty categories B, C, or D.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's accounts were unauditable for three years. However, the Category A assessment indicates the underlying issues are not systemic financial mismanagement or governance collapse, and a clear rebuild pathway exists.
findings.figures: Three consecutive years of disclaimed opinions; Category A classification
findings.quote: For the Authority this had the impact of a disclaimer of opinion issued by your predecessor auditor for the financial year 2022/23. We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 20 February 2025 to comply with the statutory backstop date as reported to you previously. For the 2024/25 audit we issued a disclaimed opinion on 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: DRAFT VFM Risk Assessment 25-26 for FARC
findings.headline: The council missed the 30 June 2026 accounts publication deadline, publishing unaudited accounts on 2 July 2026.
findings.detail: The council failed to meet the amended Accounts and Audit Regulations deadline to publish unaudited accounts by 30 June 2026, publishing two days late on 2 July. This represents a breach of law and regulations, though the assessment notes it was an improvement on the prior year and only two days late.
findings.matters: Consistent breach of statutory reporting deadlines signals compliance risk and potential weakness in financial controls and planning processes that lenders monitor.
findings.figures: 2 days late; 2 days earlier than prior year
findings.quote: By not publishing the unaudited Statement of Accounts by the required deadline, the Council has breached its laws and regulations.

findings.paper_title: DRAFT VFM Risk Assessment 25-26 for FARC
findings.headline: The 4-unitary model chosen for local government reorganisation would begin with a £22m deficit without further funding distribution.
findings.detail: Local government reorganisation creates significant medium-term financial uncertainty for the council. The selected 4-unitary council model is described as the least financially viable option and would start with a substantial deficit. The council has set aside funds to support the reorganisation but remains financially stable only in the short term.
findings.matters: A lender assessing medium-term viability needs to understand the post-reorganisation financial position. A £22m starting deficit is material and signals risk in the transition.
findings.figures: £22m deficit at vesting without further distribution of funding
findings.quote: this is considered the least financially viable option - this model would begin with a £22m deficit, without further distribution of funding

findings.paper_title: DRAFT VFM Risk Assessment 25-26 for FARC
findings.headline: Staffing recruitment and retention shortages are impacting project delivery and flagged as a significant audit risk.
findings.detail: The council faces a persistent difficulty in recruiting and retaining staff that limits its ability to deliver projects on time and forces service prioritisation. The assessment identified this as a consistent concern across senior management and a key risk on the corporate risk register. Two factors are driving this: salaries are uncompetitive with the nearby London local government market, and salaries and prospects in the private sector are more attractive.
findings.matters: A lending decision depends on whether a council can deliver its financial and service plans. Chronic understaffing that forces project delays or service cuts directly undermines delivery confidence.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: We understand there to be a number of staffing shortages at the Council which can impact on the Council's ability to deliver projects on time and leads to a requirement to prioritise key services.

findings.paper_title: FIRST QUARTER CAPITAL BUDGET MONITORING REVIEW 2026/27
findings.headline: Capital receipts shortfall will increase revenue borrowing need and MRP cost in 2027/28
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that losing the £3M capital receipts will have a revenue impact in 2027/28 by increasing the need to borrow and therefore raising the Minimum Revenue Provision charge to the General Fund.
findings.matters: This creates a known revenue budget pressure in 2027/28 that was not anticipated when the revenue budget was set.
findings.figures: £3M loss of receipts; impact materialises as increased MRP charge in 2027/28
findings.quote: This will have a revenue impact in 2027/28 as it will increase the relative need to borrow (as at 31st March 2027) and therefore lead to a higher Minimum Revenue Provision charge.

findings.paper_title: FIRST QUARTER CAPITAL BUDGET MONITORING REVIEW 2026/27
findings.headline: Positive Capital Financing Requirement of £15.162M triggers Minimum Revenue Provision charge to revenue budget from 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's CFR became positive in 2025/26 (now £15.162M at March 2026) because capital receipts did not cover the capital programme. This triggers MRP charges to the General Fund starting 2026/27, and further borrowing for capital will increase MRP charges in 2027/28.
findings.matters: MRP is a non-discretionary revenue charge that will compound as the council continues to borrow for capital, squeezing the revenue budget in future years.
findings.figures: CFR £15.162M positive at 31 March 2026; borrowing £9.851M of £13.57M capital programme (72.7%)
findings.quote: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) at 31st March 2026 was positive £15.16M. It became positive during 2025/26 as the Council did not have sufficient funding (e.g. Capital Receipts) to finance the Capital programme.

findings.paper_title: FIRST QUARTER CAPITAL BUDGET MONITORING REVIEW 2026/27
findings.headline: No capital receipts forecast for 2026/27 despite £3M assumption in Investment Strategy
findings.detail: The council's estates team review has reduced forecast capital receipts from the £3M assumed in February's budget to zero for 2026/27. One site will be let for income instead; two sites cannot be disposed while achieving best value. This removes anticipated cash to fund capital investment.
findings.matters: Losing £3M of anticipated cash flow forces increased borrowing and creates a revenue budget problem in 2027/28 through higher Minimum Revenue Provision charges.
findings.figures: £3M receipts assumed in February 2026 Investment Strategy; forecast revised to £0.0M
findings.quote: A review by the estates team means that no additional capital receipts are now forecast for this year.

findings.paper_title: FIRST QUARTER CAPITAL BUDGET MONITORING REVIEW 2026/27
findings.headline: Four capital schemes reprofiled to 2027/28 because of staff capacity constraints
findings.detail: The council has deferred £0.67M of capital spending into 2027/28, with Walsworth Common Pavilion (£0.3M) and Broadway Gardens Resurfacing (£0.25M) being the largest schemes affected. The document cites staff capacity as the explicit reason these schemes cannot start in 2026/27 as originally planned.
findings.matters: Staff capacity limits on service delivery raise questions about whether the council can execute its capital programme at all, and delays compress future spending.
findings.figures: £0.523M reduction 2026/27, £0.670M increase 2027/28; Walsworth Common Pavilion £0.3M, Broadway Gardens £0.25M
findings.quote: Based on staff capacity, the schemes listed here have been reprofiled into 27/28.

findings.paper_title: Churchgate Regeneration Project Update & Next Steps - Part 1
findings.headline: Council approval of Phase 1 does not commit to proceeding with scheme implementation
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states that approval of Phase 1 funding does not commit the council to Phase 2, a development agreement, or implementation. This staged approach allows the council to exit the project if feasibility work shows it is not viable.
findings.matters: Shows the council is attempting to limit financial exposure by reserving decision-making on later phases, but also indicates serious uncertainty about whether the project will proceed beyond feasibility study.
findings.figures: Phase 1 funding approval only; Phase 2 and implementation decisions reserved
findings.quote: Approval of this report does not commit the Council to progressing to Phase 2, entering into a development agreement or implementing any regeneration scheme. Those matters will be the subject of separate reports and future Member decisions at the appropriate time

findings.paper_title: Churchgate Regeneration Project Update & Next Steps - Part 1
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will require Shadow Authority consent for major council financial decisions from May 2027 to March 2028
findings.detail: Shadow Authorities created from May 2027 will require prior consent for 'significant financial decisions' including 'major land disposals and high-value contracts.' The paper confirms that Churchgate, as a town centre regeneration scheme, will trigger these thresholds and thus require Shadow Authority approval.
findings.matters: This creates a governance constraint on the council's decision-making autonomy during a critical period, potentially delaying major project decisions and limiting the council's ability to respond to commercial opportunities.
findings.figures: Governance constraint period: May 2027 to 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Given that the Churchgate project is a town centre regeneration scheme, irrespective of the route chosen for delivery one or more of the likely financial thresholds would be triggered and therefore any significant financial decisions between May 2027 and 31 March 2028 would require prior consent from the new Shadow Authority

findings.paper_title: Churchgate Regeneration Project Update & Next Steps - Part 1
findings.headline: Council owns shopping centre asset assessed as not commercially viable
findings.detail: The council acquired the Churchgate Shopping Centre leasehold in 2022. The paper explicitly states 'the current condition and configuration of the shopping centre are unlikely to provide a commercially sustainable long-term future,' suggesting the asset may require ongoing subsidy or eventual writedown.
findings.matters: An owned asset that the council itself assesses as commercially unviable represents a potential future call on reserves or revenue budget unless the regeneration scheme succeeds.
findings.figures: Acquisition cost and current valuation not stated
findings.quote: The Council acquired the Churchgate Shopping Centre leasehold in 2022 to support the long-term regeneration of this important town centre area, recognising that the current condition and configuration of the shopping centre are unlikely to provide a commercially sustainable long-term future

findings.paper_title: Churchgate Regeneration Project Update & Next Steps - Part 1
findings.headline: Scheme viability is finely balanced and uncertain
findings.detail: Soft market testing feedback explicitly states that 'the overall viability of the scheme remains finely balanced' and that 'further feasibility, due diligence and delivery planning work will be required before progressing towards any future delivery phase.' This indicates the council's major regeneration investment carries material commercial risk.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial position must understand that a major capital project with uncertain commercial viability could require council subsidy or create an unrecoverable asset loss.
findings.figures: Specific Phase 1 funding amount not stated in Part 1 (detailed in Part 2 report)
findings.quote: it also highlighted that the overall viability of the scheme remains finely balanced, and that further feasibility, due diligence and delivery planning work will be required before progressing towards any future delivery phase

findings.paper_title: Capital End of Year Review 2025/26, 10/06/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Multiple capital projects experiencing delivery delays: Warm Homes mobilisation delayed by landlord permission issues; Community Centres roof safety delayed after poor roof condition discovered
findings.detail: Warm Homes Local Grant project suffered mobilisation delays including difficulty obtaining landlord permission for Letchworth homes, preventing full spend of year 1 allocation (£67k underspend). Community Centres flat roof safety upgrade delayed after inspections revealed poor roof condition at one site, requiring roof assessment before proceeding with safety works (£43k underspend). Council reports pipeline for year 2 Warm Homes funding but delays indicate execution challenges.
findings.matters: Multiple project delays indicate execution and delivery challenges; suggests risk of further slippage and cost escalation across the capital programme
findings.figures: Warm Homes underspend £67k; Community Centres underspend £43k; total project-level slippage £1.161m into 2026/27
findings.quote: Underspend due to a delay in mobilisation for this project which had knock on issues (e.g. gaining landlord permission for Letchworth homes).

findings.paper_title: Capital End of Year Review 2025/26, 10/06/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Investment income erosion: as capital receipts are deployed, treasury income stream shrinks from 4.2% (£42k per £1m)
findings.detail: The council currently earns approximately 4.2% annual return (£42k per £1m) on cash reserves invested in the treasury. When capital receipts are used for capital spending and not replaced through asset sales, the amount of cash available for investment reduces, directly eroding this revenue income stream. In 2025/26 the council used £1.057m of capital receipts, reducing the cash pool earning this return.
findings.matters: Erosion of treasury investment income reduces funds available for core services and limits financial flexibility; the income stream is now dependent on maintaining capital receipts through property sales
findings.figures: Treasury returns 4.2% (£42k per £1m invested); council deployed £1.057m of capital receipts in 2025/26
findings.quote: When capital receipts are used and not replaced the availability of cash for investment reduces. Consequently, interest income from investments reduces.  £1.0million currently earns the Authority approximately £42k per year in interest (4.2%).

findings.paper_title: Capital End of Year Review 2025/26, 10/06/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement swung from negative £592k to positive £15.162m: council must now borrow externally and will incur Minimum Revenue Provision charges from 2026/27
findings.detail: At 31 March 2025 the CFR was negative £592k (indicating capital spending was covered by internal resources). One year later it is positive £15.162m. This reversal means the council can no longer fund capital investment solely from cash reserves and must access external borrowing. The council plans to initially borrow internally against cash reserves, but this borrowing will create revenue budget impact through Minimum Revenue Provision charges starting in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Shift to external borrowing requirement signals the council has exhausted available capital resources and now faces structural revenue budget pressure from debt servicing
findings.figures: CFR £15.162m positive (31 March 2026) versus £0.592m negative (31 March 2025); borrowing funded 69% of 2025/26 capital spend (£15.167m of £22.002m)
findings.quote: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) at 31 st March 2026 was positive £15.162 million (negative £0.592 million 31 st March 2025). As the CFR is now positive the Council does have a need to borrow to fund capital spend. This will have an impact on the revenue budget by way of a Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charge in 26/27.

findings.paper_title: Capital End of Year Review 2025/26, 10/06/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Leisure centre decarbonisation project overrunning by £839k; third-party legal agreement delays driving £600k in contractor and temporary boiler costs
findings.detail: The Public Sector Decarbonisation Project forecast final cost has increased by £839k. Around £600k of this is attributable to third-party land owners delaying approval of legal agreements for cables at Hitchin and Letchworth sites, which has caused contractor delays and the need to hire temporary boilers. The council reports contractors will temporarily vacate sites to minimise further cost growth. Additional minor cost drivers include seized isolation valve repairs (£114k) and substation harmonics filters (£63k).
findings.matters: Material cost escalation on major infrastructure project signals execution risk and impacts affordability of the capital programme
findings.figures: £839k total increase; approximately £600k from third-party delays; £114k isolation valve repairs; £63k harmonics filters
findings.quote: There is an increase in forecast spend by £839k on the leisure centre decarbonisation project. The main cause (around £600k) is third party delays in completion of legal agreements for cables to go across their land. This leads to increased contractor and temporary boiler costs.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Year end report on Risk Management Governance
findings.headline: Three capital projects flagged at red status: Churchgate, decarbonisation phase 2, and museum collection facility
findings.detail: The council is managing three capital projects at red risk status with severity scores of 7 or 8. Red-status projects carry implementation, cost, and delivery risk. The specific nature of each risk is detailed in Appendix A.
findings.matters: Capital projects at red risk status indicate implementation uncertainty that could lead to budget overruns, service disruption, or increased borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: Three capital projects at red status (scores 7-8)
findings.quote: three project risks (Churchgate, decarbonisation phase 2 and museum collection facility)

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Year end report on Risk Management Governance
findings.headline: Resourcing and staffing identified as the highest-scoring red risk, with specific concerns relating to Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: Resourcing is named as one of the two red risks with the highest scores in the council's risk register. A significant staffing element is tied to the LGR/Devolution risk, suggesting the council faces capacity constraints that could affect service delivery and financial management capability.
findings.matters: Staffing and resourcing capacity directly affects a council's ability to execute financial management, deliver services, and manage capital programmes—all material to creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Two red risks identified as highest-scoring: LGR/Devolution and Resourcing
findings.quote: The two risks with the highest scores relate to Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) and Devolution, and Resourcing. A significant element of the LGR risk specifically relates to resourcing/staffing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Treasury Management End of Year Review 2025/26, 10/06/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Over-investment breach: Council held £4M with single counterparty when policy limit was £3M
findings.detail: From August to December 2025 the council held £4M invested with Blackpool Council despite a £3M counterparty limit. The error occurred due to inadequate recording and checking of previous deals. The council has since implemented additional checking procedures with a second officer to prevent recurrence.
findings.matters: Breaches of internal investment limits signal control weaknesses in treasury operations, affecting lender confidence in the council's governance and financial management discipline
findings.figures: £4M actual versus £3M limit (£1M breach); breach duration 22/08/25 to 15/12/25
findings.quote: During the period ended 30 September 2025 there was an over investment with one counterparty. £4M was invested with Blackpool Council against a limit of £3M. This over-investment was for the period from 22/08/25 to 15/12/25.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Treasury Management End of Year Review 2025/26, 10/06/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Council reduced investment balances by £19.5M in a single year to fund capital expenditure
findings.detail: Investments fell from £45.0M to £25.5M as the council drew on cash reserves to finance capital projects. Of £21.975M capital expenditure, only £6.437M was financed in year, leaving £15.538M unfinanced. The council deliberately avoided new external borrowing, instead using internal borrowing (reserve drawdown).
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council is depleting contingency reserves to fund routine capital expenditure, which could constrain future borrowing capacity and financial flexibility
findings.figures: Investments fell from £45.0M to £25.5M (£19.5M reduction); unfinanced capital expenditure £15.538M; capital financing requirement rose to £14.946M
findings.quote: The level of Investments has reduced by £19.5M. This is primarily due to the large level of Capital Expenditure incurred during the year.

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET OUTTURN 2025/26 (FINAL)
findings.headline: Business Rates Collection Fund balance down £203k due to higher bad debt provision; council is managing levy and relief grant volatility
findings.detail: The Business Rates Collection Fund surplus fell from estimated £2.826m to actual £2.623m, a £203k reduction driven by higher bad debt provision. The council faces a £1.159m business rates levy from central government. It has funded this from grant held in reserve and transferred £2.861m from relief grant reserves to top up baseline funding. This shows the council is managing significant business rates volatility through reserve management rather than operational balance.
findings.matters: Business rates are volatile and the council's mitigation strategy (reserve transfers) is time-limited. If relief grant or levy baselines change, or if actual business rates collections worsen, the council may face unplanned budget pressure.
findings.figures: Business Rates Collection Fund surplus £2.623m (down from £2.826m estimate); levy £1.159m; relief grant compensation £4.562m; £2.861m transferred from relief grant reserve to top up funding
findings.quote: The Council is also subject to a business rates levy from Central Government where it collects more in business rates than the baseline determined by Central Government. The Council's business rate levy liability for 2025/26 is £1.159million. This amount has been funded from the grant held in reserve and as such has a net zero impact on the General Fund balance at the end of the year.

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET OUTTURN 2025/26 (FINAL)
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation is creating capacity constraints that are delaying multiple projects and initiatives
findings.detail: LGR is cited repeatedly as the reason for delays: IT Support projects delayed due to technical resource absorbed by LGR programme; Careline service desk solution moved to external procurement due to complexity and LGR capacity constraints; Town Centres Strategy delayed due to staff turnover; Strategic Priorities Fund carrying forward £34k for LGR-related back-fill and joint work. This shows LGR is consuming management bandwidth and causing project slippage across multiple directorates.
findings.matters: Reorganisation is degrading service delivery and deferring planned work. If reorganisation extends beyond current forecasts or outcomes disappoint, the accumulated project backlog may require additional investment or service cuts.
findings.figures: £34k carry forward for LGR costs; multiple project delays attributed to LGR resource constraints
findings.quote: Underspend relates to several planned projects to enhance business resilience and cyber security that were not completed within the financial year. Vacancies held during the year, as previously highlighted at Quarters One and Two, and the technical resource required to support the LGR programme, limited capacity to deliver the projects as planned.

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET OUTTURN 2025/26 (FINAL)
findings.headline: Planning challenge costs spiked in final quarter including Public Inquiry for 280-dwelling Barkway Road refusal
findings.detail: Legal and consultant expenditure on planning matters overran budget by £34k, with costs incurred in Q4 relating to two planning appeals: a hearing on a Traveller and Gypsy site at Pulmer Water, and a Public Inquiry for a 280-dwelling scheme at Barkway Road, Royston (refused contrary to officer recommendation). The report notes this was flagged as a financial risk when the budget was approved.
findings.matters: A large refused planning application (280 dwellings) going to Public Inquiry signals planning system stress and reputational/legal risk. The council rejected officer advice, exposing itself to appeal costs and signalling potential governance tension.
findings.figures: £34k outturn vs £84k budget overspend; Public Inquiry cost for 280-dwelling refusal
findings.quote: Further costs incurred in the final quarter relate to two planning appeals, one of which was a hearing relating to the refusal of planning permission for a Traveller and Gypsy site at Pulmer Water, and the other a Public Inquiry following the refusal, contrary to officer recommendation, of planning permission for 280 dwellings at Barkway Road, Royston.

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET OUTTURN 2025/26 (FINAL)
findings.headline: Leisure decarbonisation capital project delayed, pushing planned centre closures and income loss into 2026/27
findings.detail: The Leisure Centres Decarbonisation project overran its planned timeline. Two one-week closures originally scheduled for 2025/26 have been deferred to 2026/27. The council has carried forward £125k to offset the income impact of these future closures, indicating the decarbonisation work remains incomplete and unfunded delays are pushing revenue pressure into the next financial year.
findings.matters: Capital project delay is shifting budgeted income loss to next year, compounding 2026/27 budget pressure when leisure income is already under stress (down 9.6% year-on-year).
findings.figures: £125k carried forward to cover deferred closure impact; leisure centre visits down 1,165,547 visits
findings.quote: Two one-week closures at Hitchin and Letchworth Leisure Centres originally anticipated in 2025/26 are now scheduled for 2026/27, following the delay to the delivery of the Leisure Centres Decarbonisation project

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET OUTTURN 2025/26 (FINAL)
findings.headline: Multiple income streams in decline: burials, garden waste, commercial waste, commuted sums
findings.detail: Burial income fell £40k (trend to cremations rather than burials), garden waste subscriptions down 4.9% (32,706 vs 34,386 customers), commercial refuse customers down 5% (992 vs 1,044), and commuted sums contributions from developers fell to just two developments as developers establish their own management companies rather than contribute to council maintenance.
findings.matters: Multiple revenue sources showing secular decline (not temporary variances) suggest structural shifts in service demand. These trends compress available discretionary income and may accelerate as residents and businesses adapt their behaviour.
findings.figures: Burials down £40k; garden waste subscriptions -4.9% (32,706 vs 34,386); commercial waste customers -5% (992 vs 1,044); commuted sums fell to 2 developments
findings.quote: Commuted sums contributions income has reduced over recent years, with the outturn representing contributions to greenspace maintenance at only two developments in 25/26. Developers have taken the option to set up their own management companies to own and manage the greenspace privately, rather than transfer management responsibility to the Council and incur the cost of a commuted sum contribution.

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET OUTTURN 2025/26 (FINAL)
findings.headline: Sales ledger bad debt provision increased £50k, reflecting collection delays from financial system transition
findings.detail: Bad debt provision for sales ledger rose from £10k budget to £60k outturn. The increase is attributed to suspension of income recovery during transition to a new financial system in 2024/25, which created a backlog of aging debt. Though recovery has restarted and Q1 new debt has declined, this indicates the council faced collection challenges this year and debt quality remains impaired.
findings.matters: Collection system downtime damaged recovery momentum and increased risk exposure. Even with current recovery activity showing early signs of impact, the council acknowledged the debt position will take time to improve, signalling cash flow stress.
findings.figures: £50k increase in provision; £60k outturn vs £10k budget
findings.quote: Increase in contribution at the end of this year is attributed to the suspension of income recovery during the transition to the new financial system in 2024/25. This meant an increase in the level of outstanding debt at the end of 2024/25, with aging debt requiring a greater level of provision as the risk of non-collection increases over time.

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET OUTTURN 2025/26 (FINAL)
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves drawn down by £10.038m (net of contributions) to fund the budget
findings.detail: While the General Fund balance improved by £1.385m to £17.893m, the council transferred out £10.038m from earmarked reserves against contributions of only £5.113m. Total earmarked reserves fell from £13.7m to £8.775m. Funding from reserves (including business rate relief grant) of £2.861m was used to bridge the gap when the budget was set, indicating planned reliance on reserve drawdown rather than achievement of balance from operations.
findings.matters: Sustained reserve depletion signals the council cannot sustain its budget from current revenues and is living off reserves. When reserves become exhausted, service reductions or borrowing become necessary.
findings.figures: Transfers out £10.038m; contributions in £5.113m; net reduction £4.925m; total reserves fell from £13.7m to £8.775m; £2.861m transferred from reserves to fund the 2025/26 budget
findings.quote: A total of £5.113million has been contributed to the reserves in 2025/26 and a total of £10.038million has been transferred out of the reserves to the General Fund.

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET OUTTURN 2025/26 (FINAL)
findings.headline: Parking Penalty Charge Notice bad debt provision jumped £210k due to collection delays and system transition issues
findings.detail: Parking income exceeded budget (£927k vs £573k), but the council also increased bad debt provision by £210k to cover higher-risk outstanding PCN debt. The increase follows suspension of income recovery during a financial system transition in 2024/25, which aged the debt portfolio and reduced recovery rates. While Q1 recovery activity shows debt is improving, current year pressure is significant.
findings.matters: Bad debt spikes indicate collection weakness beyond the budgeting cycle. Reliance on a one-time system transition explanation masks the underlying recovery challenge and raises questions about whether debt collection will return to prior baselines.
findings.figures: £210k increase in PCN bad debt provision; £372k contribution (outturn) vs £162k budget; PCN income £927k vs budget £573k
findings.quote: Higher levels of PCN activity over the last several years has contributed to the increase in the calculated contribution required to the bad debt provision at the end of this financial year. The suspension of income recovery during the transition to the new financial system also affected the age profile of the outstanding debt, with greater provision required for debts aging over that period to recognise the increased risk of non-collection.

findings.paper_title: REVENUE BUDGET OUTTURN 2025/26 (FINAL)
findings.headline: Leisure centre visitor numbers down 9.6% with significant management fee income shortfall
findings.detail: Leisure centre visits fell to 1,558,505 from 1,724,052 in the prior year. The management fee income came in at £321k against a budget of £714k—a £393k shortfall (red status). The decarbonisation project was delayed, pushing two planned one-week centre closures from 2025/26 into 2026/27, and £125k is being carried forward to offset the impact of those future closures.
findings.matters: A sustained 9.6% decline in leisure usage signals weakening consumer discretionary spending in the district and risks further income pressure in the next financial year, particularly as closure-related income loss has been deferred rather than absorbed.
findings.figures: 1,558,505 visits (2025/26) vs 1,724,052 (2024/25); £321k outturn vs £714k budget; £125k carried forward; £393k shortfall
findings.quote: Two one-week closures at Hitchin and Letchworth Leisure Centres originally anticipated in 2025/26 are now scheduled for 2026/27, following the delay to the delivery of the Leisure Centres Decarbonisation project

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 and Action Plan for 2026/27
findings.headline: Complaint volume surged 54% from 384 in 2023/24 to 591 in 2024/25
findings.detail: The council and its contractors received 591 complaints in 2024/25, up from 384 in 2023/24 (54% increase). The majority (66%, or 391 complaints) relate to services delivered by key contractors, particularly the leisure contract (370 complaints) and waste/recycling (21). The sharp rise suggests operational or service quality degradation.
findings.matters: A 54% surge in complaints signals operational stress or service failure; concentrated complaints in leisure and waste suggest execution issues with major contracts, which may require remediation spending or contract renegotiation.
findings.figures: 591 complaints in 2024/25 vs 384 in 2023/24; 370 leisure centre complaints; 21 waste and recycling complaints; 66% attributable to contractors
findings.quote: The number of complaints received by both the Council and our contractors increased from 384 in 23/24 to 591 in 24/25 (a 54% increase). Of the total 591 complaints, 391 (66%) relate to services delivered by our key contractors including our waste and recycling contract (21) and the leisure centres (370).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 and Action Plan for 2026/27
findings.headline: Resourcing crisis: staff shortages and recruitment difficulties rated as top risk (score 9)
findings.detail: Resourcing is identified as a top-level risk (9 out of 9) driven by staff shortages and difficulties recruiting to some areas. This affects the council's ability to deliver projects within the Council Delivery Plan. The Building Control company annual review did not occur in 2025 due to resourcing issues.
findings.matters: Staff shortages directly impact service delivery, project execution, and financial controls; if core functions (audit, finance, compliance) are under-resourced, financial governance and risk management weaken.
findings.figures: Resourcing risk score 9 on matrix; Building Control review did not occur in 2025
findings.quote: Resourcing has remained as a score of 9 on the risk matrix... It also refers to staff shortages and difficulties in recruiting to some areas. The annual review of the Building Control company did not occur in 2025 due to resourcing issues.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 and Action Plan for 2026/27
findings.headline: Fraud referrals remain elevated at 113 in 2024/25, higher than pre-pandemic levels
findings.detail: The council received 113 fraud allegations in 2024/25, similar to 2023/24 (117) but materially higher than pre-pandemic levels. Housing benefit and council tax fraud accounted for 78 of the 113 cases; housing fraud was the second largest category with 19 cases. This suggests control weakness in benefits and housing administration.
findings.matters: Persistently elevated fraud (above pre-pandemic) indicates either control deficiencies in benefits/housing or increased vulnerability; both matter for financial stability and operational risk.
findings.figures: 113 referrals in 2024/25; 117 in 2023/24; 78 housing benefit and council tax; 19 housing fraud
findings.quote: During 2024/25 there had been 113 'referrals' (allegations) of fraud affecting council services. It was reported that this was very similar to the previous year where there were 117 referrals, but higher compared to pre-pandemic levels. The main type of fraud being reported in the 2024/25 period was related to housing benefit and council tax, with this accounting for 78 referrals.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 and Action Plan for 2026/27
findings.headline: Churchgate shopping centre regeneration project is high-risk and affordability is questioned
findings.detail: Churchgate is a major regeneration scheme for a shopping centre and surrounding areas. It is rated as a high-risk project (score 8). The specific risks flagged are affordability of the regeneration and potential failure to meet stakeholder expectations — both suggest the financial model may be under strain.
findings.matters: Large capital regeneration projects carry execution and cost overrun risk; affordability concerns suggest the project may require subsidy, draw on reserves, or increase borrowing beyond budget.
findings.figures: None provided on project cost or funding gap
findings.quote: The Churchgate project refers to plans to regenerate a shopping centre and the surrounding areas. It is a high-rated risk, with the risk relating to the affordability of the regeneration, and the possibility of failing to meet the expectations of stakeholders.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 and Action Plan for 2026/27
findings.headline: Leisure Centre Decarbonisation poses revenue loss risk from full or partial facility closure
findings.detail: The council is undertaking decarbonisation work and a gym extension at Royston leisure centres. This capital project carries a specific risk: full or partial closure of facilities during works will reduce revenue from leisure services, impacting both income and cash flow.
findings.matters: Leisure centre income is an operational revenue source; a multi-year partial closure with no compensating income is a direct hit to cash flow and may require reserve drawdown or borrowing to cover the gap.
findings.figures: None provided on quantum of revenue loss
findings.quote: The risk around Leisure Centre Decarbonisation includes a financial risk around loss of revenue due to full or partial closure of the Council's leisure centres while the decarbonisation and gym extension (Royston) works take place.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 and Action Plan for 2026/27
findings.headline: Financial Sustainability identified as the council's top strategic risk, scored 9 out of 9
findings.detail: The council's risk register identifies Financial Sustainability as one of four top strategic risks at the highest score (9). The statement notes that while the MTFS, budgets and capital programme are soundly based, ongoing financial pressure remains the leading concern facing the authority.
findings.matters: Top-level financial sustainability risk indicates the council is aware of budget pressure; lenders need to understand whether this is structural and whether the MTFS credibly addresses it.
findings.figures: Financial Sustainability risk scored 9 on risk matrix
findings.quote: In the Mid-Year Risk Governance update reported to Finance Audit and Risk Committee in January 2026, the top risks (scoring a 9 on the risk matrix) for the Council were Financial Sustainability, Local Government Reorganisation, and Resourcing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 and Action Plan for 2026/27
findings.headline: Two audits received limited assurance in 2024/25, covering Estates and Houses in Multiple Occupation
findings.detail: Of 21 internal audits completed in 2024/25, two returned limited assurance opinions (meaning control weaknesses identified). Seven high-priority recommendations were made across all 2024/25 audits. Limited assurance typically indicates material control deficiencies requiring urgent remediation.
findings.matters: Limited assurance findings flag specific areas where management controls are weak; if these relate to financial reporting or housing (which affects revenue and risk), they matter for credit decisions.
findings.figures: 21 audits completed in 2024/25; 2 limited assurance; 0 substantial assurance; 9 reasonable assurance; 7 high-priority recommendations made
findings.quote: 21 audits were completed in 2024/25, 0 had substantial assurance, 9 had reasonable assurance, 2 had limited assurance... The limited assurance opinions related to Estates and Houses in Multiple Occupation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 and Action Plan for 2026/27
findings.headline: Two high-priority internal audit recommendations remain outstanding at end of 2025/26
findings.detail: Despite completion of most audit recommendations, two high-priority findings have not been resolved and management has provided revised implementation dates. These represent unaddressed control weaknesses in the council's systems.
findings.matters: Outstanding high-priority audit findings indicate management is not closing control gaps promptly; this suggests either control deficiencies are harder to fix than anticipated or remediation is not prioritised.
findings.figures: 2 high priority recommendations outstanding at end of 2025/26
findings.quote: In respect of the progress of management in implementing high priority internal audit recommendations, two remained outstanding at the end of 2025/26, with revised implementation dates provided by management.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025/26 and Action Plan for 2026/27
findings.headline: External auditors issued a disclaimed opinion on 2024/25 accounts, unable to complete audit work
findings.detail: KPMG has issued a disclaimed opinion for 2024/25 accounts, continuing from the 2022/23 position. This means the auditors could not undertake enough work to form a view on the truth and fairness of the accounts. The council attributes this to national audit backlog outside its control, but the impact is that accounts remain unaudited.
findings.matters: Unaudited or disclaimed accounts increase credit risk; lenders cannot rely on external audit verification of financial position, and the multi-year delay suggests persistent audit capacity issues.
findings.figures: 2022/23 audit opinion disclaimed; 2024/25 audit opinion disclaimed
findings.quote: As the 2022/23 audit opinion was disclaimed, it was not possible for KPMG to undertake enough audit work to issue an unqualified opinion. Instead, they have issued another disclaimed opinion.

findings.paper_title: KPMG Audit Plan & Strategy 2025-26
findings.headline: Local Government Pension Scheme triennial valuation requires material accounting changes; some councils now in pension surplus with complex recognition rules
findings.detail: The new triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025 requires re-basing of the council's estimate models to allow for actual experience since 2022. This could result in corrections to the defined benefit obligation and asset valuations. KPMG notes that recent market changes have caused increasing numbers of councils to move into or increase pension scheme surplus, and that "the requirements of the accounting standards on recognition of these surplus are complicated and requires actuarial involvement."
findings.matters: Pension liability is typically the largest balance sheet item; the triennial valuation reset combined with potential surplus recognition creates material accounting uncertainty that could significantly affect reported financial position.
findings.figures: Triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025; pension liability component subject to actuarial assumptions
findings.quote: small changes in the assumptions and estimates used to value the Council's pension liability could have a significant effect on the financial position of the Council.

findings.paper_title: KPMG Audit Plan & Strategy 2025-26
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio of £27.7m held at fair value with significant estimation risk each year
findings.detail: The council holds investment property valued at £27.7m as at 31 March 2025. KPMG has identified valuation of investment property as a significant audit risk because fair value assessment requires significant judgment; the carrying amount could materially differ from fair value, particularly where market conditions change.
findings.matters: This is a material asset base; misstatement of valuation directly affects the balance sheet and could conceal deterioration in asset values that affects borrowing capacity or reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: £27.7m as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The portfolio had a value of £27.7m as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: KPMG Audit Plan & Strategy 2025-26
findings.headline: Extensive rebuilding assurance work must be completed by 31 July 2026 before final audit sign-off, testing all prior years' account balances
findings.detail: To restore audit confidence, KPMG is conducting a comprehensive rebuilding assurance risk assessment including reconciliation of planned reserve movements from budget setting and outturn reports, assessment of capital addition/disposal processes, and balance sheet financial statement assessment of movements over the entire disclaimed period, overlaid with findings from other risk assessment procedures.
findings.matters: The rebuilding assurance work creates additional delay and cost before the 2025/26 audit can be signed off; completion deadline of 31 July 2026 means final audit sign-off will not occur until later than normal, extending the period of unverified accounts.
findings.figures: Completion deadline: 31 July 2026
findings.quote: As part of the 2025/26 audit we are in the process of completing by 31 July 2026 our rebuilding assurance risk assessment which includes: Reconciling the planned movement in reserves from budget setting, in year monitoring and outrun reports and documenting our understanding of planned usage and changes in reserves over the disclaimed period.

findings.paper_title: KPMG Audit Plan & Strategy 2025-26
findings.headline: Three consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions—auditors cannot verify the council's financial statements are accurate
findings.detail: The council has received disclaimed audit opinions for 2022/23 (predecessor auditor), 2023/24 (issued 20 February 2025), and 2024/25 (issued 27 February 2026). A disclaimer is the most serious audit outcome and means the auditors have insufficient evidence to form an opinion on whether the financial statements present a true and fair view.
findings.matters: No external auditor verification of the council's financial position, assets, liabilities or reserves creates material uncertainty for any lender assessing creditworthiness or for the council's own financial planning.
findings.quote: For the Authority this had the impact of a disclaimer of opinion issued by your predecessor auditor for financial year 2022/23. We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 20 February 2025 to comply with the statutory backstop date as reported to you previously. For the 2024/25 audit we issued a disclaimer of opinion on 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: THIRD QUARTER REVENUE BUDGET MONITORING 2025/26, 25/03/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Burial grounds income declining due to competition from new private crematorium
findings.detail: Burial grounds income is £39k short with ongoing impact of £42k into 2026/27. The council attributes decline to industry-wide trend from burials to cremations, and specifically to competition from a new private crematorium at Holwell. Hitchin Cemetery is now at capacity for burials, potentially driving residents to the competing facility.
findings.matters: Structural shift in customer demand and new competition reducing a council income stream, with capacity constraints in the council's own facility exacerbating loss of market share
findings.figures: £39k shortfall 2025/26; £42k ongoing impact 2026/27
findings.quote: Shortfall in income is attributed to the trend, apparent across the industry, away from full body burials to cremations. The Council only receives income from cremations if the family choose to purchase a grave space or a memorial tree within a North Herts Cemetery. With Hitchin Cemetery now at capacity for burials, the Council may also be losing custom to the new crematorium at Holwell, which offers cremations, cremated remains and full burial grave spaces. Some Hitchin residents may therefore be choosing this option in preference to Wilbury Hills Cemetery.

findings.paper_title: THIRD QUARTER REVENUE BUDGET MONITORING 2025/26, 25/03/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Increased project slippage with £710k of carried-forward budgets expected unspent
findings.detail: Budgets carried forward from 2024/25 total £1.682m. By Q3, forecast unspent is £710k (up from £526k at Q2), an increase of £184k. This represents slippage across 8 projects including Local Plan review (£67k), transport policy (£56k), supplementary planning documents (£76k), and Careline telephone upgrade (£20k). Reasons cited include supplier resourcing issues, MHCLG delays in publishing legislation, and procurement delays.
findings.matters: Persistent project delays across multiple work streams suggest either resource constraints, poor project management, or external dependencies creating delivery risk for medium-term plans
findings.figures: £710k forecast unspent of £1.682m carried forward; £184k increase from Q2 forecast
findings.quote: At Quarter Two, it was forecast that £526k of the budget carried forward will not be spent in this year. At the end of Quarter Three it is forecast that £710k of the budget carried forward will not be spent. The increase of £184k, all of which is requested to be carried forward again into 2026/27, relates to: Careline telephone lines upgrade... Royston Town Council Annexe Redevelopment... Riverside walk, Hitchin... Climate change strategy... Supplementary Planning documents... Local Plan review... London Luton Airport Development Consent Order application... Transport policy projects and initiatives... Housing stock condition survey.

findings.paper_title: THIRD QUARTER REVENUE BUDGET MONITORING 2025/26, 25/03/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Leisure centre income performance significantly below budget with unsettled compensation claim
findings.detail: Leisure centre management fee income is flagged RED in financial health indicators with projected outturn of £196k against budget of £714k (£518k variance). The actual position is distorted by a pending compensation claim to the leisure service provider for closure during decarbonisation works, which has not yet been settled. Leisure centre visits are up 0.9% year-on-year.
findings.matters: Major income line performing at 27% of budget with an unsettled liability suggests either significant contractual disputes, poor budget accuracy, or other material issues with the leisure contract
findings.figures: £196k projected outturn vs £714k budget (£518k variance); 1,317,474 visits vs 1,305,810 prior year (+0.9%)
findings.quote: The actual to date exceeding the projected outturn for leisure centres management fee income in table 4 is because the compensation to the leisure service provider for the closure of the leisure centres while the decarbonisation works took place, as reported at Quarter Two, has not yet been settled.

findings.paper_title: THIRD QUARTER REVENUE BUDGET MONITORING 2025/26, 25/03/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Commercial waste service income declining with ongoing structural impact
findings.detail: Commercial waste and recycling customer income is forecast £30k short in 2025/26 with an ongoing impact of £30k into 2026/27. Customer base has declined 5.9% year-on-year. The council attributes this to competitive market pressure, businesses switching providers with introductory pricing, economic downturn, and efficiency improvements by customers reducing waste. This was identified as a financial risk at budget approval.
findings.matters: Declining revenue from a significant council service (£1.267m budget) with structural drivers suggests ongoing income pressure in future years, not a temporary variance
findings.figures: £30k shortfall 2025/26; £30k ongoing impact 2026/27; customer base down 5.9% to 955 customers
findings.quote: Forecast shortfall in income follows the steady decline in the size of the customer base, as has been captured in the corporate financial health indicators included in previous monitoring reports. This may be indicative of a competitive market, where businesses are incentivised to switch provider with introductory pricing for new customers; changes in business behaviours to generate less waste in general, with existing customers reducing the level of service required; a difficult economic climate more generally. A shortfall in income from Commercial Waste services due to an economic downturn was identified as a financial risk when the original budget was approved in February 2025.

findings.paper_title: THIRD QUARTER REVENUE BUDGET MONITORING 2025/26, 25/03/2026 Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Churchgate regeneration project has insufficient funding for consultant costs
findings.detail: Consultant expenditure is forecast at £163k overspend to complete due diligence on the project. The paper states the council planned to fund this from surplus rent income and a reserve, but forecasts this is not sufficient. This underfunding was identified as a financial risk when the budget was approved in February 2025.
findings.matters: A major regeneration capital project is already running over budget in its planning phase, indicating either scope creep or underestimated costs, which raises questions about final project viability and full lifecycle costs
findings.figures: £163k overspend on consultant expenditure; original budget for this line was £0k
findings.quote: While part of the spend in this year will be funded from surplus rent income collected (over and above the cost of capital related to the purchase of the head leasehold) and the balance remaining in the Churchgate Regeneration Project earmarked reserve, the variance indicates that this is not sufficient to fund the forecast level of expenditure. This was identified as a financial risk when the budget was approved in February 2025.

findings.paper_title: THIRD QUARTER CAPITAL BUDGET MONITORING REVIEW 2025/26
findings.headline: Large capital programme reprofiling (£3.066M): 15% of spending pushed to following year due to delays, resource constraints, and design phases
findings.detail: The largest reprofiling is Public Sector Decarbonisation (£732k), delayed due to change in delivery approach from single contractor to multiple services with specialist sub-contractor. Other delays cite lack of resources (Cycle Strategy, Transport Plans, Green Infrastructure), design completion times, and external funding uncertainty (Oughtonhead Weir). Collectively this indicates stretched delivery capacity.
findings.matters: Chronic project delays suggest the council may have insufficient staff capacity or expertise to manage its capital programme at pace, creating execution risk for future schemes and potential for further cost overruns.
findings.figures: Total 2025/26 reprofiling: £3.066M decrease; 2026/27 impact: £3.011M increase; largest single scheme: Public Sector Decarbonisation Phase 2 (£732k)
findings.quote: The Project Board for the Decarbonisation Phase 2 project agreed at their meeting in September 2025 to a change in delivery approach moving from having a single tier one contractor managing the whole project to directly appointing individual services to produce designs and then a specialist mechanical and electrical contractor to deliver the works.

findings.paper_title: THIRD QUARTER CAPITAL BUDGET MONITORING REVIEW 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital spending erodes investment income: revenue fund will lose approximately £40k per year as capital receipts are deployed
findings.detail: Each £1M of capital receipts deployed generates approximately £40k per year in lost investment income. As the council is now using capital receipts to finance the programme (£1.273M used in 2025/26), this income will decline materially and must be absorbed by the general fund.
findings.matters: A finance director managing a constrained revenue budget needs to account for declining investment income; for a lender, it signals shrinking discretionary cash generation and tighter financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £1.0M in capital receipts currently generates £40k per year; 2025/26 capital receipts used: £1.273M
findings.quote: £1.0M currently earns the Authority approximately £40k per year in interest. The general fund estimates are routinely updated to reflect changes in income from investments.

findings.paper_title: THIRD QUARTER CAPITAL BUDGET MONITORING REVIEW 2025/26
findings.headline: Avenue Park Splash Park held pending viability review: original design does not match market practice
findings.detail: The council has paused the £70k project pending investigation into feasibility. The original proposal relies on mains water whereas modern splash parks use recycled/recirculated systems. The council has put spending on hold to reassess whether the project is viable.
findings.matters: Project pauses and design rework delays revenue recovery from capital investment and may indicate governance gaps in capital scheme appraisal at approval stage.
findings.figures: Paused spend: £70k; 2025/26 forecast: £0k of £70k budget
findings.quote: The project is under review while further investigation is undertaken. We are reviewing how splash parks are typically designed/operated and in particular the water source. This current proposal relies on mains water, whereas most modern splash parks are designed to use recycled or recirculated water systems. The funding has not been spent whilst we assess if the project is viable.

findings.paper_title: THIRD QUARTER CAPITAL BUDGET MONITORING REVIEW 2025/26
findings.headline: Priory Gardens Bandstand needs rebuild instead of renovation; budget raised from £50k to £75k
findings.detail: The original capital budget was for bandstand renovation, but inspection has revealed it needs complete replacement. The budget has been increased by £25k to £75k for 2026/27. This suggests asset condition assessment was incomplete or conditions have deteriorated.
findings.matters: Unplanned increases in scope suggest asset condition may be worse than the council's fixed asset registers reflect, with implications for other building assets in the portfolio.
findings.figures: Original budget £50k → revised budget £75k; increase of £25k
findings.quote: The original budget was to renovate the Bandstand. The bandstand however needs replacing and the budget needs increasing to allow this project to proceed in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: THIRD QUARTER CAPITAL BUDGET MONITORING REVIEW 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement turned positive: council must now borrow for capital spending
findings.detail: The CFR shifted from negative £0.59M to positive during 2025/26, meaning the council no longer has sufficient capital receipts to self-fund its capital programme. It will now need to borrow, with MRP charged to the general fund from 2026/27 onwards. This represents a material change in the council's capital financing position.
findings.matters: A shift from self-sufficient capital funding to requiring external borrowing signals tighter financial headroom and new debt servicing costs that will constrain future revenue budgets and affect financial resilience.
findings.figures: CFR at 31 March 2025: negative £0.59M; 2025/26 forecast spend: £23.350M; borrowing in capital programme: £16.334M
findings.quote: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) at 31st March 2025 was negative £0.59M. It has become positive during 2025/26 as the Council does not have sufficient funding (e.g. Capital Receipts) to finance the Capital programme. This means the Council will have to borrow to fund the programme in this year, with MRP (Minimum Revenue Provision) charged to the General Fund in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Royston Leisure Centre learner pool absorbs £4.002m—69% of the entire 2027/28 capital programme
findings.detail: The council plans £750k in 2026/27 and £4,002k in 2027/28 for a new learner pool at Royston Leisure Centre. When total capital expenditure in 2027/28 is forecast at £5,787k, this single discretionary leisure project represents nearly 70% of all planned capital spending.
findings.matters: Heavy concentration of capital on a single non-essential leisure facility, while financial reserves are being drawn down 82%, raises questions about capital prioritisation during a period of increasing financial pressure
findings.figures: Royston Learner Pool: £750k (2026/27), £4,002k (2027/28); total 2027/28 programme: £5,787k
findings.quote: Royston Leisure Centre Learner Pool 750 4,002

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Cash available for treasury investment declines 82% in four years, from £16.5m to £2.9m
findings.detail: Funds available for investment fall from £16,451k at end of 2025/26 to £2,988k by end of 2028/29. This reflects deployment of reserves for internal borrowing to fund the capital programme, draining the council's liquidity buffer.
findings.matters: Declining liquidity reduces capacity to absorb financial shocks, self-fund emergencies, or take advantage of opportunities. Lower balances also reduce investment income that offsets borrowing costs
