findings.paper_title: Appendix A Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Financing costs as percentage of net revenue budget swing from -8.2% (surplus) to 8.3% over five years
findings.detail: In 2025/26, investment income exceeds financing costs (shown as -8.2% of budget). From 2026/27 this reverses due to Minimum Revenue Provision charges and borrowing costs. By 2030/31, financing costs reach 8.3% of revenue budget as the Capital Financing Requirement grows and cash reserves decline.
findings.matters: A 10-point swing indicates significant growing pressure on the council's operational budget, materially reducing financial flexibility and headroom
findings.quote: Financing Costs as a % of Net Revenue Budget: 2025/26 -8.2%, 2026/27 3.4%, 2030/31 8.3%

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Stevenage Leisure Ltd liquidation resulted in £308k bad debt write-off on fitness equipment loan
findings.detail: The council made a £308k loan to Stevenage Leisure Ltd for gym equipment. Covid-19 impacts led to a repayment holiday; while SLL resumed paying management fees in 2023/24, it could not repay the loan. The company entered liquidation in July 2024 with the loan still outstanding, triggering a full bad debt provision.
findings.matters: Demonstrates credit loss on a commercial leisure investment, showing financial stress in a key service delivery partner
findings.figures: £308k full bad debt provision
findings.quote: As at the end of the contract in March 2024 the loan remained unpaid and SLL went in to liquidation in July 2024.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Section 25 report
findings.headline: Pension contribution rate increases possible after 2029/30 triennial valuation
findings.detail: Pension costs have reduced significantly, contributing materially to the council's improved financial position. This reduction is based on long-term funding horizons, past-service contributions, and strong investment performance. However, the CFO cautions that the next triennial valuation (after 2029/30) could reverse this with higher contribution rates.
findings.matters: Pension contributions are fixed and non-negotiable; a sudden increase would constrain service budgets without recourse to efficiency or demand management. The council should model the 2029/30 impact now.
findings.figures: Triennial valuation date 2029/30; no quantified risk given
findings.quote: However, it is worth noting that there is some risk that the next triennial valuation could see an increase in contribution rates. However that would not apply until 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Section 25 report
findings.headline: Housing demand pressures ongoing despite grant increases; subsidy loss risk requires quarterly monitoring
findings.detail: Housing is the main service area with demand pressures, primarily from hotel and B&B placements for homeless. Specific housing grants have increased and cover current excess costs. However, there is a subsidy loss risk where Housing Benefit reclaimed from DWP falls short of amounts paid to providers.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled housing placement demand could quickly exceed grant funding, forcing the council to absorb costs. Subsidy loss exposure grows with inflation and vacancy patterns.
findings.figures: No specific figures given; identified as main demand pressure area requiring quarterly monitoring
findings.quote: Housing is the main service area where we see demand pressures, which usually result in an increase in the need to use hotel and B&B placements. The excess cost of these placements is currently being covered through specific housing grants... But it remains an area to keep a focus on through quarterly monitoring, including the impact of subsidy loss.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Section 25 report
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) funding not guaranteed and modelled to decline 20% annually
findings.detail: The council treats EPR funding as part of base funding for waste collection and disposal. However, the CFO explicitly notes this funding is not guaranteed. Current assumptions model a 20% annual reduction, though the CFO cautions this needs review because collection costs are linked to property numbers, not volumes.
findings.matters: EPR funds cover costs already in the base budget; a shortfall would either require compensating savings or reduce waste service standards. The forecast reduction could total £1m+ over 5 years if linear.
findings.figures: Assumed 20% annual reduction; funding treats packaging collection and disposal as baseline cost
findings.quote: However, this funding is not guaranteed, and the aim is that it will reduce packaging volumes. The current assumption is that the funding will reduce by 20% each year. This will need to be kept under review, as collection costs are linked to number of properties rather than volumes.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Section 25 report
findings.headline: Pay inflation forecasts at 3% may be insufficient; economic data shows public sector pay inflation running higher
findings.detail: The council increased pay inflation forecasts to 3% for 2026/27 and 2027/28. However, the CFO explicitly notes that economic data is showing pay inflation in other parts of the public sector exceeding these levels. The waste and street cleansing contract is still awaiting confirmation of pay award impact from April 2025.
findings.matters: Pay typically comprises 40-50% of council operating costs; even 0.5% forecast error creates material budget variance. Underestimating pay inflation cascades across multiple service areas.
findings.figures: 3% pay inflation assumption; current public sector inflation observed above this level
findings.quote: Pay inflation forecasts were increased to 3% for 2026/27 and 2027/28. Even with this increase, this may not be sufficient, particularly for 2026/27. Economic data is showing that pay inflation in other parts of the public sector are higher than these levels.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Section 25 report
findings.headline: Business Rates reset creates £240k income risk as safety net reduces from historic above-baseline position
findings.detail: The council has previously been above baseline funding with minimal Business Rates risk. The reset removes this advantage. While there is a 0% safety net in 2026/27 (no immediate risk), the safety net increases to 7.5% in later years, creating exposure to variances in collected Business Rates income.
findings.matters: A £240k income loss would require compensating service cuts or material reserve drawdown, directly affecting the council's financial stability and debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: £240k potential risk identified
findings.quote: The reset will create some risk, depending on the level of Business Rate income that is collected compared to the baseline. As there is a 0% safety net in 2026/27 there is no risk next year. But the risk increases as the system moves back towards a 7.5% safety net. The risk could be around £240k.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C: KPMG Year End Report (ISA 260) to the Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Pension scheme net surplus increased by £19.7m year-on-year to £26.8m, triggering complex surplus recognition accounting under IFRIC 14
findings.detail: The Local Government Pension Scheme moved from a £7.1m surplus in 2024 to £26.8m in 2025. This significant movement requires specialist actuarial assessment for proper accounting treatment under IFRIC 14. The auditor confirmed the treatment is consistent with prior year but acknowledges the requirements are 'complicated'.
findings.matters: Volatile pension surplus swings (279% increase) indicate market sensitivity and create accounting uncertainty. The treatment depends on complex actuarial assumptions and IFRIC 14 nuances, creating potential for misstatement. This materially affects the council's net asset position and reserve classifications.
findings.figures: 2024 pension surplus: £7.1m; 2025 pension surplus: £26.8m; Year-on-year increase: £19.7m (279%)
findings.quote: The scheme reports a net surplus of £26.8 million as at 2025 (2024: £7.1 million). Recent changes to market conditions have meant that more councils are finding themselves moving into surplus in their Local Government Pension Scheme (or surpluses have grown and have become material). The requirements of the accounting standards on recognition of these surplus are complicated and requires actuarial involvement.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C: KPMG Year End Report (ISA 260) to the Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: High Needs accommodation provider partnership resulted in suspended Housing Benefit payments in March 2025 due to unresolved regulatory status
findings.detail: Since December 2021, the council entered an agreement with a High Needs provider that initially caused subsidy loss. The provider registered as a Housing Association in May 2023 to access higher Housing Benefit rates. However, the provider's Regulator of Social Housing status remained 'for-profit' despite assurances. The council suspended benefit payments in March 2025. No written requirement or deadline was set for the provider to achieve the required status.
findings.matters: Suspended benefit payments represent service delivery risk and reputational exposure. The arrangement demonstrates governance weakness in partnership agreements (no written terms, no deadline enforcement). The ongoing proceedings with the provider represent contingent liability exposure and potential financial loss.
findings.figures: Benefit payments suspended as of March 2025; ongoing proceedings; Cabinet report scheduled November 2025
findings.quote: In December 2021, the Authority made an agreement with a High Needs accommodation provider, initially resulting in subsidy loss for the Authority. The provider registered as a Housing Association in May 2023, aiming to access higher Housing Benefit rates and to eliminate subsidy loss to the Authority. However, the provider's Regulator of Social Housing status remained 'for-profit' despite assurances from the provider that it would change, leading to the Authority to suspend benefit payments in March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C: KPMG Year End Report (ISA 260) to the Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: £48k revaluation adjustment to Churchgate Shopping Centre improperly credited to reserve without reversing prior impairment losses
findings.detail: The upward revaluation of Churchgate Shopping Centre (£48k) was credited directly to the Revaluation Reserve without first reversing prior impairment losses that had been previously recognised. This represents incorrect application of accounting standards.
findings.matters: Property valuations are a significant part of the council's asset base. Incorrect reserve accounting treatment obscures the true financial position and suggests incomplete control over major assets. This is particularly relevant given Churchgate's prominence in the council's commercial property portfolio.
findings.figures: £48k upward revaluation of Churchgate Shopping Centre
findings.quote: We have reperformed the calculations of the movements in value of land and buildings and identified that the upward revaluation movements of £48k for Churchgate Shopping Centre was credited directly to the Revaluation Reserve without first reversing prior impairment losses previously recognised.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C: KPMG Year End Report (ISA 260) to the Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Four significant control deficiencies identified, including ineffective management review controls over major asset valuations
findings.detail: Auditing standards require KPMG to report that management review controls for asset valuations (land and buildings, investment property, pensions) are ineffective. Additionally, the journals review process within the council's general ledger system is reported as ineffective. These are systemic control environment weaknesses.
findings.matters: Ineffective controls over valuations and transaction authorization are foundational risks. They indicate management may not detect or prevent material misstatements in property and asset bases (totalling over £250m combined). This is particularly concerning given the 2024 general ledger system migration.
findings.figures: 4 significant control deficiencies; asset valuations affected: Land & Buildings £75.8m, Investment Property £27.7m, Pension liabilities (143.5m)
findings.quote: Auditing standards require us to report that the design and implementation of the management review control relating to this area is ineffective in line with the ISA definition.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C: KPMG Year End Report (ISA 260) to the Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: £867k uncorrected misstatement in pension assets testing, representing 13.8% of the annual deficit
findings.detail: During testing of defined benefit pension assets, KPMG identified a material variance of £867k. This remains unadjusted in the financial statements. The pension scheme reports a net surplus of £26.8m as at 2025, up from £7.1m in 2024.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements in the council's largest balance sheet items (pension liabilities/assets) indicate audit gaps and potential financial position understatement. The material variance in pension accounting, combined with the significant year-on-year surplus increase, creates uncertainty over the true financial position.
findings.figures: Uncorrected misstatement: £867k (13.8% of deficit); Pension surplus moved from £7.1m (2024) to £26.8m (2025)
findings.quote: A material variance of £867k was noted and an uncorrected misstatement has been raised.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C: KPMG Year End Report (ISA 260) to the Finance, Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Auditor has disclaimed opinion on the financial statements due to insufficient evidence over reserves and balance sheet items
findings.detail: Due to the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026, KPMG determined there is insufficient time to obtain audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 and 2024. The auditor states this is 'pervasive to the Authority's financial position' and has led to a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements as a whole.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion signals that fundamental financial position uncertainties exist and cannot be verified. Lenders rely on audited accounts; a disclaimer substantially increases credit risk assessment uncertainty.
findings.figures: Statutory backstop date: 27 February 2026; opening balances and reserve movements unverified
findings.quote: Given our work to rebuild assurance is not complete and due to the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026, we have determined that there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 ahead of the backstop, and, in our view, this is pervasive to the Authority's financial position as at 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A- Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-30
findings.headline: Pay inflation assumption increased from 2% to 3% for 2026/27 and 2027/28, driven by National Living Wage and pay catch-up
findings.detail: Council raised pay assumption to reflect ongoing above-target inflation and National Living Wage pressure on bottom pay scales, which forces consequential uplifts to maintain differentials. No decision made on discretionary pay rises beyond NJC settlements, but cost pressure is explicit and quantified at additional £0.4m (2026/27) and £0.8m (2027/28).
findings.matters: Pay is the largest cost in local government. A 1% swing in pay assumptions across the council adds material pressure. This is a real cost that is now hitting the budget gap.
findings.figures: Pay inflation uplift: £0.4m (2026/27), £0.8m (2027/28 onwards)
findings.quote: It is proposed that this assumption is changed to 3% for 2026/27 and 2027/28. This is to reflect that: General inflation will remain above the 2% target over that period. Increases in the National Living Wage are likely to create pressure on our pay levels. This will have the greatest impact on those at the bottom of the pay scales, but we have to be mindful on maintaining pay differentials.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A- Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-30
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (packaging) income declining 20% annually; £1.44m reduces to £0.59m by 2030
findings.detail: EPR is volatile and unpredictable. The policy aims to reduce packaging waste, which in theory reduces collections but does not reduce collection costs (which are per-household, not per-volume). Simultaneously, loss of recyclable material volumes reduces sale income from materials. Council assumes 20% annual decline without modelling upside if waste reduction stalls or market prices shift.
findings.matters: A revenue stream that is declining by design and cannot be reliably forecast. By 2029/30 it will contribute only £0.59m. This is structural income erosion that adds to the deficit problem without the council having control over it.
findings.quote: The aim of EPR is to encourage reductions in packaging waste so over time the payments we receive should slowly decrease. Reductions in packaging waste that needs to be collected will not reduce our costs as collection costs are priced based on number of households, not volumes collected. It is possible that net costs could go up as some of the recyclable material that we collect generate an income, which is linked to volumes. We will need to forecast how much our EPR payments will be in future years. We will base this on a 20% reduction each year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A- Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-30
findings.headline: LGR preparation has consumed all government seed funding; additional budget required for 2026/27 with scope unclear
findings.detail: Local Government Reorganisation (council ceases 1 April 2028) is 'very resource intensive'. Government's initial funding is 'all been used'. Council expects to need additional budget for IT, HR and other support areas in 2026/27, but no quantum is stated and the work is described as likely to 'continue', not finish.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council is managing a controlled merger or whether LGR is consuming management time and budget in ways that distract from financial control. The vagueness about the scope and cost of LGR work is itself a risk signal.
findings.figures: LGR funding from Government: fully consumed. 2026/27 budget requirement: to be quantified.
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) This has been very resource intensive in supporting the development of the options proposal document, alongside the consultant support. It is expected that this will continue and likely to need additional resource in key support areas (e.g. IT and HR). The initial funding from Government has all been used. There will need to be additional budget allocated as part of the 2026/27 budget process, although this will be time-limited.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A- Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-30
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation grant (£370k per year) to be rolled into general funding, creating unfunded pressure
findings.detail: Currently a specific grant netted against service spend. Government intends to roll it into Fair Funding formula. The council must now budget this as a revenue pressure but has no offsetting saving identified. This adds £370k to the budget gap.
findings.matters: Homelessness pressures are rising nationally. A lender sees this as an ongoing cost that will now sit on the general fund balance sheet. If homelessness demand increases, the council has no specific ring-fenced funding to absorb it.
findings.figures: £370k per year from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: The Temporary Accommodation element of the Homeless Prevention Grant has been a specific grant, and therefore netted off against the expenditure in that service area. As detailed above the intention is that this grant will be rolled in to general funding. So the service budget will need to be increased to reflect the loss of direct grant funding. This is a pressure of £370k each year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A- Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-30
findings.headline: Pension contribution rates expected to decrease in December 2025 valuation, but council is still forecasting based on 2022 valuation
findings.detail: Current forecasts use contribution rates set by 2022 triennial valuation (effective to 2025/26). New valuation results due December 2025 will set rates for 2026/27–2028/29. Indications suggest rates may decrease, but this is not yet factored into the strategy.
findings.matters: Pension costs are a fixed commitment and a material part of the council's spend. If valuation shows improvement, it provides some relief to the budget gap. If indications prove wrong, it is another pressure the council has not yet flagged.
findings.figures: Current forecasts based on 2022 valuation effective to 2025/26. New valuation due December 2025.
findings.quote: The latest triennial valuation (for March 2022) was completed before the 2022/23 budget was set. That valuation set our pension contribution rates for the three years up until 2025/26. Current forecasts for 2026/27 onwards are also based on that valuation. We expect to get our funding results by December, which will set our contribution rates for the next three years (2026/27 to 2028/29). Indications have been that we could see a decrease in these costs.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A- Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-30
findings.headline: Capital reserves fully depleted; council moving to borrowing for capital spend
findings.detail: The council has used all capital reserves and must now borrow to fund capital expenditure. Initially plans to use internal borrowing (drawing on cash balances held for investment), which carries an opportunity cost (lost interest) and Minimum Revenue Provision charge. This is noted as 'a normal position for Councils' but marks a change in the council's balance sheet and borrowing requirement.
findings.matters: A lender sees a council that has shifted from capital reserves to borrowing. Internal borrowing is cheaper short-term but exposes the council if cash positions tighten or if the authority moves to external borrowing. The cost assumptions (no 'significant changes in treasury or MRP costs') may not hold if interest rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: Capital reserves: fully depleted. Treasury assumptions: based on 2025/26 forecasts with no increase assumed.
findings.quote: We have moved to a position where we have a need to borrow to fund our capital programme, as we have used up all our capital reserves. This is a normal position for Councils to be in, and there are provisions that allow us to borrow to fund capital spend.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A- Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-30
findings.headline: Structural budget gap of £1.5m–£2.4m in 2026/27, potentially £3.4m by 2028/29, with no credible savings plan
findings.detail: Even with £14.8m in reserves, the council faces a persistent gap between forecast spend (£23.3m rising to £24.2m) and estimated funding. Council states that 'most of the efficiency savings have been taken' and remaining options 'likely require changes to service levels'. Residents prefer new funding sources, not cuts, but these are not identified.
findings.matters: The council is banking on either reserves drawdown or service reductions. Reserves are adequate for short-term but not sustainable. A lender needs to know whether management has a credible path to a balanced budget or whether the unitary merger (2028) is being treated as a way to push the problem forward.
findings.quote: It is difficult to commit to a package of savings to address the higher funding gap, when the lower funding gap is so much smaller. As a result of the level of savings we have delivered previously, most of the efficiency savings have been taken and remaining savings are likely to require changes to service levels.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A- Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-30
findings.headline: Fair Funding 2.0 creates £2.6m swing in funding by 2028/29 depending on whether social care grants are kept outside the general pot
findings.detail: Government consultation on funding reform leaves outcome unclear until December 2025 settlement. Council's models show funding could range from £4.86m to £7.46m in 2028/29 depending on social care treatment. This swing is the single largest variable in the council's financial planning.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council is borrowing into structural weakness (if social care stays separate) or relative stability. The council cannot commit to a savings plan while the range is this wide.
findings.figures: With Social Care in baseline 2028/29: £7.46m; Without: £4.86m; Difference: £2.60m
findings.quote: The most significant one of these is whether social care grants are treated as part of the general funding pot to be allocated or kept outside to be allocated on a more specific social care formula. Making it part of the overall funding pot means that we get a very small share of it. But as it is such a large amount of grant, that very small share is significant.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B- Potential General Fund Balance forecasts
findings.headline: Forecast funding carries wide variance—up to £2.65m annually—creating significant uncertainty in which scenario materialises
findings.detail: The council's funding is projected across a range rather than a point, with spreads of £0.87m in 2026/27 expanding to £2.65m by 2029/30. This uncertainty drives the divergence between positive and negative cases, meaning the council faces material risk that the worse case will occur.
findings.matters: Large funding volatility makes financial planning uncertain and forces councils to hold larger reserves to manage risk. It indicates exposure to factors beyond council control.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B- Potential General Fund Balance forecasts
findings.headline: Persistent annual budget gaps of £1.53-£3.38m across all four years, with council assumed to deliver no savings to close them
findings.detail: The forecast shows structural gaps between spending and funding ranging from £1.53m to £2.40m (positive case) and £2.40m to £3.38m (negative case) each year. The analysis explicitly assumes the council does not deliver savings, meaning these gaps are bridged by drawing down reserves rather than by addressing underlying spending or raising income.
findings.matters: Budget gaps funded from reserves rather than resolved through savings indicate weak structural finances and planning. This is not sustainable and constrains the council's flexibility for future pressures.
findings.quote: assuming that the Council does not deliver any savings. This is against a likely recommended (by Chief Finance Officer) minimum General Fund reserve balance of £3 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B- Potential General Fund Balance forecasts
findings.headline: In the negative funding case, reserves fall from £19.6m to £7.53m by 2029/30, reaching approximately 1.5 years from the minimum threshold
findings.detail: Under worst-case funding, the council's General Fund balance declines by over 60%, from £19.6m at start of 2026/27 to £7.53m by 2029/30. While still above the CFO-recommended minimum of £3m, the trajectory leaves only 1.5 years at that point before potentially breaching the minimum. Even the positive case shows reserves falling to £15.39m—a reduction of £4.2m over four years.
findings.matters: Rapidly depleting reserves signal financial stress and leave a council with minimal capacity to absorb spending pressures or unexpected costs. Proximity to minimum thresholds is a key indicator of financial vulnerability for lenders.
findings.figures: Negative case: £19.6m → £17.2m → £13.88m → £7.53m across four years; 60% reduction; CFO minimum: £3m; Positive case end: £15.39m
findings.quote: In the negative case, the overall reserves are still above the minimum level in 2029/30 but have reduced by over 60%, and are about 1.5 years away from going below the minimum level.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2030 Addendum for Cabinet
findings.headline: Pay and contract inflation together add £0.70m to £1.40m annually to revised forecast spend.
findings.detail: Pay inflation contributes £0.40m in 2026/27 and £0.80m from 2027/28 onwards. Contract inflation contributes £0.30m in 2026/27 and £0.60m from 2027/28 onwards. These are additional recurring costs beyond the 2025/26 baseline, and fees-and-charges income offsets only £0.20m–£0.40m of this.
findings.matters: Structural inflationary pressures make real-terms savings harder to achieve and increase the difficulty of balancing budgets without service reductions.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2030 Addendum for Cabinet
findings.headline: Annual budget gaps of £1.53m to £3.38m exist across the MTFS period if the council delivers no savings.
findings.detail: This is a baseline scenario explicitly assuming zero savings delivery. Budget gaps range from £1.53m–£2.40m in 2026/27, peak at £0.78m–£3.38m in 2028/29, then narrow to £0.32m–£2.97m by 2029/30. The council's actual financial plan depends entirely on closing these gaps through savings.
findings.matters: Undisclosed or unachievable savings plans mean these deficits will materialise and be covered by reserve drawdown, accelerating the depletion risk shown in the negative case.
findings.quote: This is against a likely recommended (by Chief Finance Officer) minimum General Fund reserve balance of £3 million. [assuming that the Council does not deliver any savings.]

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2030 Addendum for Cabinet
findings.headline: Under negative funding assumptions, General Fund reserves fall from £19.6m to £7.53m by 2029/30, breaching minimum thresholds within 1.5 years thereafter.
findings.detail: The addendum models reserve impact under two scenarios. The positive case reduces reserves to £15.39m by 2029/30 (manageable). The negative case reduces them to £7.53m — a 61% reduction from starting level. At that depletion rate, the council would breach the CFO's recommended minimum of £3m by approximately 2030-31.
findings.matters: Reserve erosion below minimum thresholds forces spending cuts or borrowing; this trajectory shows the council has limited headroom to absorb funding shocks or failed savings plans.
findings.figures: Starting reserves: £19.6m; Negative case 2029/30: £7.53m (reduction of £12.07m); CFO minimum: £3m; runway to minimum threshold: 1.5 years
findings.quote: In the negative case, the overall reserves are still above the minimum level in 2029/30 but have reduced by over 60%, and are about 1.5 years away from going below the minimum level.

findings.paper_title: FIRST QUARTER TREASURY MONITORING REVIEW
findings.headline: Interest income forecast is £1.0M above budget at £1.825M for the full year
findings.detail: The council forecast £1.825M of investment interest for 2025/26, representing an increase of £1.0M on the original budget. This outperformance is based on treasury performance in the first three months, during which the council maintained average investments of £50.0M, generating £0.906M in interest. The council holds a conservative investment portfolio (47% local authorities, 37% government, 16% banks) with very low credit default risk across all positions.
findings.matters: Outperforming interest income by £1.0M improves budget flexibility and reduces financial pressure on the council, which directly affects financial sustainability and credit quality for lenders
findings.figures: £1.825M full-year forecast; original budget implied at £0.825M; £1.0M variance above budget; £50.0M average investment balance; £0.906M interest generated in first three months; average interest rate 4.51% (down from 5.1% at 31st March)
findings.quote: This is an increase of £1.0M on the original budget.

news_drafts.headline: Commercial waste and recycling income red-flagged: £12k shortfall driven by ongoing structural decline in customer base
news_drafts.lead: A key revenue line is in structural decline despite regulatory changes; income from this source may continue to erode

news_drafts.headline: IT development projects deferred by Local Government Reorganization: £45k of planning software budget carried forward for second year
news_drafts.lead: LGR is causing material disruption to planned technology investments and business improvements; carry-forward for a second year suggests these may not proceed at all

news_drafts.headline: Efficiency programme running 2% behind target at end of Quarter One: £59k net underachievement against £2.894m plan
news_drafts.lead: Efficiency savings are critical to the financial plan; early-year shortfalls suggest the council may miss annual targets and face funding pressure
